Happy World Toilet Day -- a celebration of all things pottyYahoo for the loo! November 19 marks the 25th anniversary of World Toilet Day. The theme this year: "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures."
Jack Sim, the founder of World Toilet Day, travels the world promoting access to safe and clean toilets. When NPR photographed him a few years ago — on a toilet, of course — he was glad to oblige even though it was a chilly and windy November day.
John Poole/Ryan Kellman/NPRhide caption
John Poole/Ryan Kellman/NPR
Twenty-five years ago, Jack Sim was flush with excitement. (Please pardon the pun.)
The Singapore entrepreneur was looking for a meaningful project and came upon this thought from the prime minister: "He said we should measure our graciousness according to the cleanliness of our public toilets," Sim recalls.
Thus was born World Toilet Day. The goal was more than cleanliness. It was access, too — billions of people do not have a safe and sanitary toilet to use.
Enshrined as an official U.N. day in 2013, World Toilet Day aims to get people talking and thinking about a topic that maybe is a taboo in polite conversation.
A rally in India calls for decent sanitation on a past World Toilet Day demonstration.
NOAH SEELAM/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
hide caption
NOAH SEELAM/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
Let's eschew the euphemisms
World Toilet Day is all about peeing, pooping and addressing menstrual hygiene in a clean and safe manner — followed by the "conveyance" of excreta to a sanitary disposal system, notes Kate Olive Medlicott, the sanitation and waste team leader within the WASH team at the World Health Organization. Human diseases are shed in sewage, so a top-notch sanitation system is critical, says Medlicott. Cholera is linked to sewage. Polio is, too.
This year's World Toilet Day theme is "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures." Even though everyone suffers when they can't find a toilet, the menstrual cycle creates additional complications. If schools or offices lack a safe and sanitary place to attend to period needs and to dispose of period products, girls and women may opt to stay home.
There is another gender issue. Sofia Calltorp, the U.N. Women global head of humanitarian action, says: "When women and girls do not have access to safe toilets," they leave their home and look for a public toilet or a secluded space to do their business, often venturing into unsafe areas. "There is a huge impact in terms of being exposed to harassment or violence," Calltorp says. She points to refugee camps as a place where this issue often arises, with unlit toilets that aren't differentiated by gender.
Poo Guru is a character created by the Defeat Diarrheal Disease Initiative in its ongoing campaign to educate the world about sanitation and the need for safe toilets for all.
DefeatDDhide caption
DefeatDD
In Western Colombo, Sri Lanka, an informational sign urges users not to squat on the seat as though they were using a squat toilet, which often consists of ... a pit.
Haag/ullstein bild/via Getty Images
hide caption
Haag/ullstein bild/via Getty Images
A sign from Valencia, Spain, is a reminder of how important it is to have access to a safe toilet.
Kristina Ketelsenhide caption
Kristina Ketelsen
Now you might well ask: Has World Toilet Day made a difference?
The toilet titans we interviewed say yes, it has, just by talking about toilets in the public arena. The U.N. has stated that access to safe sanitation is a human right. And in just about every country, progress has been made in improving access to sanitary facilities. Since 2015, 1.2 billion people have become part of the world of safely managed sanitation systems.
What are the next steps? Kellogg Schwab, who specializes in water and wastewater contaminants of public health concern at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, stresses that governments should be a force for change but that it shouldn't be top down. It should also be … oh, forgive me again … bottom up. Schwab suggests giving money to communities to figure out what solutions they can come up with to improve the toilet and sanitation situation. There will be flops. But there will be successes that can be scaled up.
Sand artist Sudarsan Pattnaik created this sculpture in honor of World Toilet Day on a beach in the coastal city of Puri in India. Like the contents of a toilet connected to a sanitation system, it was ... washed away.
NurPhoto/via Getty Images hide caption
NurPhoto/via Getty Images
So maybe one day — Medlicott of WHO thinks in 50 years or so —- Earthlings will look back and say, How curious that in a world of wealth there were not enough safe and secure toilets.
A toast to toilets
Let's end by reflecting on the present day.
"World Toilet Day is my favorite day of the year," says Medlicott. "People find it fun and funny but it's really important to celebrate and act on something we take for granted."
If you're among the population where toilets are plentiful, she suggests pausing to think of a moment — it's happened to all of us — when you needed a bathroom and couldn't find one. Maybe that incident has turned into a funny story you share with friends. Now imagine if it were to happen every day.
I am deeply thankful that all I need to do is walk down the office hallway to find a clean and private loo.

With intensifying climate change, extreme temperatures are becoming more common across the globe. Such extreme temperatures represent an urgent public health challenge that warrants both effective environmental and energy policy. Previous studies have linked both extreme heat and extreme cold to higher mortality risks, which are projected to grow as climate change increases the frequency and severity of temperature extremes. Addressing these threats requires effective climate adaptation measures, including ways to help people maintain safe indoor temperatures.
Households commonly rely on cooling devices, such as air conditioning, to protect against temperature extremes. However, the effectiveness of this practice relies largely on energy affordability. When energy prices rise, households may opt to cut back on cooling, increasing their risk of exposure to unhealthy indoor temperatures. Increasing global energy prices, due to inflation or geopolitical issues, can further worsen this burden. Consequently, there is an urgent need for developing solutions that can ensure people's access to effective climate control while preventing energy-related poverty.
In a recent study, Assistant Professor Yi-Chun Ko from the Asian Growth Research Institute and Professor Shinsuke Uchida from the Faculty of Policy Studies at Doshisha University, Japan, explored how residential solar photovoltaics (PV) can mitigate the mortality risks associated with extremely hot temperatures by reducing dependence on the power grid. "Air conditioning protects people during extreme heat, but only if households can afford to run it," explains Prof. Uchida. "While the environmental benefits of distributed renewable energy adoption are well established, we provide the first causal evidence that household solar PV can also work as a public health intervention, reducing heat-related mortality through improved energy affordability." Their study was made available online on October 12, 2026, and published in Volume 410 of Social Science & Medicine in December 2026.
To investigate the impact of household solar PV systems, the researchers leveraged a unique natural experiment created by the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake, which resulted in the shutdown of nuclear power plants and, consequently, electricity price increases of up to 38%. During the same period, rooftop solar infrastructure was also promoted through a nationwide subsidy program in Japan.
The researchers combined monthly prefecture-level mortality data from 44 prefectures (excluding Iwate, Miyagi, and Fukushima, which were directly hit by the earthquake and tsunami) between 2009 and 2014 with high-resolution weather data and official records of residential solar PV installations. Households that install solar PV systems might differ from those that do not in terms of factors like housing quality, energy efficiency investments, environmental preferences, or broader climate adaptation strategies, all of which could independently affect mortality. To isolate the effect of solar PV systems, the researchers used an instrumental variable (IV) strategy within a two-stage least-squares framework. The instrument combines long-term regional differences in solar radiation, which make solar panels more productive in sunnier areas, with lagged regional electricity prices, which increase the savings from self-generated power, to identify the causal effect of solar PV adoption on temperature-related mortality.
The results showed that residential solar PV adoption significantly reduces mortality associated with extreme heat, with the greatest impact observed among older individuals aged 65 and above—the demographic most vulnerable to extreme temperatures. Using the annual average growth rate of solar PV installations during the study period, the researchers estimated that the excess deaths caused by each extremely hot day were reduced by approximately 8.2% per year for the population as a whole, and by 8.5% per year among adults aged 65 and older. The team also found that the protective effects were stronger in prefectures that are warmer, experienced higher post-2011 electricity price spikes, and faced stricter energy conservation targets. In contrast, no comparable effects were observed at cold temperatures, which is consistent with the fact that solar panels generate most power during sunny, hot summers.
These patterns point to a clear mechanism: solar panels make it more affordable for households to keep running air conditioners when cooling is most needed. Consistent with this, prefectures with more solar installations purchased less electricity from the grid on hot days. A placebo analysis further supported this interpretation. Specifically, the protective effects were concentrated in cardiovascular mortality, which is highly sensitive to heat stress, while no statistically significant effects were observed for accident-related deaths.
These findings indicate a previously underexplored strategy through which renewable energy could enhance climate resilience. "Rooftop solar can serve as an effective adaptation strategy against heat-related health risks, on top of its well-known benefits of reducing emissions and enhancing energy security," remarks Prof. Ko.
However, the benefits may not be distributed equally. The researchers found that solar PV adoption tends to be concentrated in higher-income areas, while the renewable energy surcharge that funds the feed-in tariff for solar power raises electricity prices for all households. Additionally, households without air conditioning or those unable to install panels—such as renters and apartment dwellers—may not benefit directly. The researchers stress the need for targeted policies to reduce inequality and ensure that public health protections reach vulnerable populations.
"Our findings show that homes that generate their own electricity can become part of the infrastructure that protects public health," notes Prof. Uchida. "With effective policies, residential solar adoption could make societies both greener and more resilient, while narrowing rather than widening health inequalities."
The researchers note that the findings come from a period of unusually sharp electricity price increases in Japan, when self-generated electricity was especially valuable; similar situations can arise during other energy price shocks, such as those following the Russia–Ukraine conflict. Overall, this study presents distributed household renewable energy adoption in a new light, highlighting its potential not only to enhance energy independence but also to improve public health.
About Professor Shinsuke Uchida from Doshisha University, Japan
Dr. Shinsuke Uchida is currently a Professor at the Faculty of Policy Studies at Doshisha University. He received his Master's degree from University College London, UK, in 2002 and his Ph.D. from the University of Maryland, USA, in 2014. His research interests include applied econometrics, climate change, natural disasters, and environmental issues in health, agriculture, and economic development. He is a recipient of the 2022 Nagoya City University International Research Collaboration Award and the 2018 University of Verona Internationalisation Programme CooperInt award.
About Assistant Professor Yi-Chun Ko from Asian Growth Research Institute, Japan
Dr. Yi-Chun Ko is currently an Assistant Professor at the Asian Growth Research Institute. She received her Master's degree and Ph.D. from Tohoku University in 2018 and 2022, respectively. She also serves as a visiting researcher at Tohoku University and a part-time lecturer at Nagoya City University. Her research focuses on environmental economics and applied econometrics, particularly the impacts of climate change and adaptation mechanisms in agriculture, energy, and health. She received the NERPS Best Presentation Award and the Best Speed Talk Award from the Society for Environmental Economics and Policy Studies in 2022.
Funding information
This study was conducted under the 2024–2025 Basic Research Project at the Asian Growth Research Institute. This study was also supported by the Grants-in-Aid for Scientific Research (C) (23K01379) of the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science, by the Environment Research and Technology Development Fund (JPMEERF20S11821) of the Environmental Restoration and Conservation Agency of Japan, and by a research grant from the Murata Science and Education Foundation.

articles.title: Don't forget workers delivering essential services during drought: FPSA - Fiji Sun

articles.full_text:
The Fiji Public Service Association (FPSA) has urged the Government not to forget the frontline workers working tirelessly to keep essential services running as Fiji battles the worsening El Niño-induced drought.
While welcoming the Government's $20 million emergency relief allocation, the association warned that workers delivering critical services also faced extreme heat, water shortages and increasing workloads.
FPSA general secretary Judith Kotobalavu said the Government's response did not adequately address the protection, welfare and working conditions of public sector employees responsible for implementing disaster response measures.
The concerns follow the Prime Minister's declaration of a National State of Disaster in response to the escalating drought.
The $20 million allocation is intended to support emergency relief, water supplies, agriculture and affected communities.
However, the FPSA said greater attention must be given to workers in health, water services, agriculture, local government and other essential sectors.
These employees are expected to face additional emergency duties, prolonged exposure to extreme heat and water shortages while maintaining services for affected communities.
The association identified critical gaps in the Government's response, particularly access to safe drinking water at workplaces, overtime compensation, emergency duty allowances and adequate staffing.
It also called for financial assistance for affected employees and employment protection where drought conditions disrupt normal operations.
The FPSA highlighted the particular challenges facing workers in remote and maritime communities, where additional safeguards were needed.
The association urged the Government to establish a dedicated Workers' Protection and Welfare Framework.
The proposed framework would ensure safe working conditions, appropriate compensation, adequate resources, targeted financial assistance and protection of workers' employment rights throughout the disaster and recovery period.
The FPSA stressed that public sector workers were also affected by the drought and should not be expected to maintain essential services at the expense of their own health, safety and welfare.
“A national disaster response cannot be comprehensive if it protects communities but overlooks the workers responsible for delivering that protection.”

How much Dogecoin you need to be a millionaire by 2030 depends on its future price. For instance, you would need about 4 million DOGE if the price reaches $0.25, while only 1 million DOGE would be needed if it hits $1.
Dogecoin (CRYPTO: DOGE) is trading at approximately $0.058, meaning that $1 million buys around 17,217,038 DOGE. The coin has dropped 27.3% in the last month and 64.2% over the past year, hitting a one-year low on November 14. It trades 92.1% below its all-time high.
Banks and major analysts haven’t published an official 2030 price prediction for Dogecoin, so this article examines four potential price points: $0.25, $0.50, $1, and its previous all-time high. So how many DOGE would each level take, and which ones look reachable?
Dogecoin Would Need a $156.8 Billion Market Value to Reach $1
Market value equals the price multiplied by the total number of coins in circulation. Dogecoin’s market value stands at around $9.09 billion, placing it 13th among cryptocurrencies. To reach each target price, the market would need to value Dogecoin at least four times higher.
Among the four price levels, $0.25 appears most achievable, as Dogecoin has traded above this price point in the past. Its monthly high was $0.27 in October 2025, and it reached $0.43 in January 2025. Dogecoin also came close to $0.50, peaking at $0.48 in December 2024.
However, Dogecoin set an all-time high of $0.73 on May 7, 2021, while $1 is above any price Dogecoin has ever reached. A look at what it could take for Dogecoin to reach $1 by 2030 covers that level in more detail.
About 5 Billion New Dogecoin a Year Raises Every Target by 2030
Dogecoin has no maximum supply limit and issues around 5 billion new coins every year as mining rewards. At this rate, the total supply could rise to about 177 billion DOGE by the end of 2030, about 13% more than the current circulation of 156.8 billion.
An increase in the number of coins available at any given price raises the total market value. Consequently, each target price listed would necessitate a larger market value by 2030 than the figures in the table. For Dogecoin to reach $1, the market would need to value it at around $177 billion. This means more investment would be required just to maintain any given price because the supply of coins keeps increasing.
This reasoning illustrates why regaining the all-time high may be more complicated than it seems. In May 2021, when Dogecoin hit $0.73, fewer coins were in circulation, so that price required a lower market value than it would now. Additionally, Dogecoin trades below its 200-day moving average of $0.08, a sign of a challenging trend for holders.
How Much Dogecoin Do You Need to Be a Millionaire by 2030?
For most investors, reaching a $1 million Dogecoin portfolio by 2030 would likely require a substantial initial investment—possibly in the six-figure range. The $0.25 target appears most realistic, requiring around 4 million DOGE, costing about $232,328 at its price. The $0.50 mark might be achievable in a robust market cycle, but a new all-time high or $1 seems unlikely by 2030, given the supply growth and this year’s 50.7% decline.
First, Dogecoin must overcome the $0.08 moving average, which is 38% above its price, then break above the September 22 high of around $0.10. If Dogecoin surpasses $0.10, a move toward $0.25 could become a realistic discussion. However, if it continues to struggle below $0.08 into 2027, even the $0.25 target could become elusive, as 3 reasons to buy Dogecoin before 2027 and 2 reasons to wait also weigh.
Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst and the editor of 24/7 Wall St.'s Crypto Desk, where he covers Bitcoin, XRP, Ethereum, Solana and the altcoins investors search for most. His work focuses on price levels, spot ETF flows, on-chain data and the regulatory decisions that move crypto markets, written so a first-time buyer and a seasoned trader can both use it.
Sam has written about crypto professionally since 2019 and has published more than 2,000 articles. Before joining 24/7 Wall St., he wrote for crypto media outlets and Web3 companies and ghostwrote for crypto founders and token launches. His analysis is syndicated on Yahoo Finance, MSN and AOL and has been cited by other crypto news sites. He also founded MacLabs Marketing, a content and personal branding agency for crypto founders and executives.
When he isn't reading charts, Sam is usually at the gym or watching One Piece, a series he maintains has better tokenomics than most altcoins.
